first.rationale: Two of the three current problems (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%) are funnel-mechanics problems, and the inherited record points most directly at onboarding/signup friction (memory_86, memory_31) as the lever with compounding effect on both. Promotional pricing (memory_73) is the tempting response to the competitor's entry pricing, but the objective is sustainable long-term qualified revenue: discount-led acquisition tends to buy price-sensitive, low-retention accounts and resets price expectations, and memory_73 as summarized only reports acquisition and revenue lift, not retention or margin over time. Referral incentive (memory_57) is a healthy-base play and the base is currently degrading; enterprise sales-assist (memory_44) does not touch the two metrics that are actually falling. I want the archived source records for memory_86 and memory_31 because they are the load-bearing evidence for my intended action and both have a known failure mode: memory_31 explicitly worked by cutting required fields at signup, which can lift first-week activation while degrading lead qualification data, routing, and downstream conversion to qualified revenue. The summaries measure activation and completion, not revenue quality, so the summary may be true and still not support the objective. I also want to know whether the memory_86 result was measured on self-serve accounts only and whether either lift persisted past the measurement window or decayed, and whether the current declines share a cause with the original conditions (day 12 and day 52 baselines may predate the competitor's entry and any recent funnel changes). If verification shows the lift came primarily from stripping qualification fields, I will shift the test toward sequencing/deferring fields rather than deleting them, or fall back to activation_messaging (memory_91), which improves engagement without touching lead data. Because the inherited findings are summaries of older conditions and the environment has changed on day 76, I am scoping this as a small guarded test with downstream qualified-revenue and lead-quality metrics instrumented alongside completion and activation, not a broad rollout on the strength of the summary alone.

mid.rationale: Verification largely supported the intended action and, importantly, separated the two mechanisms. exp_86 (shortening the onboarding flow) is the clean one: completion +13%, time-to-value -2.1 days, and 30-day retention +3% — the lift did not come at the expense of downstream quality, which is exactly the failure mode I was worried about. exp_31 (cutting required signup fields) is weaker evidence: activation +9% and qualified revenue +4%, but 30-day retention -1%, and explicitly not replicated outside SMB. So I am running simplify_onboarding built on the exp_86 mechanism — resequencing and shortening the flow, deferring rather than deleting qualification fields — and treating exp_31 as supporting-but-bounded evidence rather than a license to strip the signup form. This addresses both falling metrics at once (onboarding completion -4% and, via time-to-value, activation -6%) and is the only candidate whose verified record shows a retention-positive result, which matters more than raw lift given the objective is sustainable long-term qualified revenue. I am declining promotional_pricing despite the competitor's entry pricing: memory_73 remains unverified, its summary reports acquisition and revenue lift with no retention or margin figure, and discount-led response to a price attack risks buying exactly the churn-prone accounts that degrade long-term qualified revenue. Remaining uncertainty I am not resolving with this decision: exp_86 dates to day 52 and exp_31 to day 12, both plausibly predating the competitor's entry, and neither record tells me the cause of the current quarter-over-quarter declines — the declines could be mix-shift from losing price-sensitive SMB accounts rather than genuine funnel regression, in which case an onboarding fix will underperform its historical effect size. I am therefore running this as a standard controlled experiment rather than a broad rollout, instrumented on qualified revenue, lead-routing quality, and 30-day retention alongside completion and activation, segmented SMB vs. other since exp_31 explicitly failed to replicate beyond SMB. If qualified revenue or retention moves negative even while completion rises, I stop and reconsider rather than scaling. activation_messaging (memory_91) is the fallback if this reads flat.

final2.rationale: Holding the decision. The new information is real and urgent, but it does not change which evidence is strong, and urgency is not a reason to spend the one non-carrying experiment slot on the weakest-supported option. Three reasons I am not switching to promotional_pricing. First, memory_73 is unverified and I can no longer verify it this cycle; its summary reports acquisition and revenue lift with no retention, margin, or durability figure — precisely the gap that verification exposed in memory_31 (activation +9% and qualified revenue +4%, but retention -1%). Second, and most decisive: memory_73 is about acquiring price-sensitive SMB prospects, and today's problem is retaining existing SMB accounts in churn conversations. Those are different mechanisms, and the inherited record does not actually cover the case I would be applying it to. Third, matching a competitor who has already cut twice invites a third cut; a discount-led response to a deeper-pocketed price attack resets our price expectations permanently and buys back exactly the lowest-retention revenue, which is the direct opposite of sustainable long-term qualified revenue. By contrast simplify_onboarding rests on the one record verification came back clean on: exp_86, completion +13%, time-to-value -2.1 days, 30-day retention +3% — lift with no downstream quality cost. Faster time-to-value is also a defensible retention lever against a price attack, since accounts that reach value quickly are less likely to be won by price alone. I am building on the exp_86 mechanism (resequencing and deferring fields) rather than exp_31's field-stripping, which showed negative retention and did not replicate outside SMB. Separately, and outside this slot: the doubled churn conversations are a commercial and account-management problem, not an experiment. Targeted retention offers, contract-term concessions, or save plays for named at-risk accounts can be run by the sales and success teams today without consuming the experiment capacity, and that is what I would recommend to leadership as the response to the price cut. Uncertainty I am carrying and not resolving: exp_86 dates to day 52 and predates the competitor's entry, so its effect size may not transfer under current conditions; the current -6% activation and -4% completion may be mix-shift from losing price-sensitive accounts rather than true funnel regression, which would make this test read flat. I will instrument qualified revenue, 30-day retention, and lead quality alongside completion and activation, segmented SMB versus other, and stop rather than scale if retention or qualified revenue moves negative. If the read is flat, activation_messaging (memory_91) is next, and I will spend next week's verification budget on memory_73 before any pricing action.
